Tax instalments need a payment calendar: setting money aside is not the same as paying CRA

Use a fixed 2026 example to connect quarterly payment dates with month-end reserve transfers, then identify the cash needed before each deadline.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore a fixed 2026 quarterly instalment cash calendar

Interactive planning lab

Four entered instalment payments$20,000
Additional cash needed at the start to fund every payment date$3,000
Reserve balance after the December month-end transfer-$2,000

Fixed 2026 educational calendar for the ordinary quarterly individual-instalment pattern, using independently confirmed payment amounts. CRA lists March 15, June 15, September 15 and December 15, with next-business-day receipt when a due date falls on a weekend or recognized holiday. The March 15 date is Sunday in 2026, so this calendar uses Monday March 16; the other three modeled dates remain the fifteenth. Reserve transfers occur on actual calendar month-ends, after that month’s mid-month payment. Starting reserve earns zero. A transfer into your own reserve is not a payment to CRA. The model does not establish an obligation, determine instalment amounts, select a calculation option, settle final annual tax, calculate interest or penalties, cover farming/fishing or deceased-person exceptions, or guarantee payment-processing time. Check applicable provincial or territorial holiday effects before applying the reference dates. No later-year calendar is inferred. Negative balances are unfunded requirements; no borrowing is assumed.

The central idea

A reserve transfer funds your own account. An instalment payment leaves it. Match the two schedules and test the lowest balance before relying on a year-end total.

01

Keep the reserve account and the tax-payment record separate

A household can regularly set money aside for tax without having sent that money to the tax authority. The reserve is a funding arrangement inside the household. An instalment is an actual payment on a separately confirmed schedule. Treating the reserve transfer as if it were tax already paid can hide both a payment obligation and the cash needed to meet it.

The example begins on 1 January 2026 with CAD 6,000 assigned to instalments. It adds CAD 1,000 at each calendar month-end and pays four independently entered CAD 5,000 instalments. These amounts are hypothetical. The tool does not calculate them from income or determine whether a person is required to pay instalments.

Use the actual applicable payment amounts before applying a personal calendar. Keep bank transfers into a reserve distinct from confirmed payments to CRA and retain evidence of the latter.

02

State the calendar year and the date rule

The CRA due-date page lists March 15, June 15, September 15 and December 15 for most individuals required to pay quarterly instalments for 2026. Its weekend and recognized-holiday rule uses receipt on the next business day.

March 15 is a Sunday in 2026. This reference calendar therefore uses Monday March 16, followed by June 15, September 15 and December 15. The example is fixed to 2026; it does not silently roll these dates into another year. The CRA public-holiday page also notes that provincial and territorial holidays can affect due dates, so verify the applicable circumstances.

The ordinary quarterly pattern is the scope of this exercise. Farming/fishing and deceased-person exceptions, a different authority’s payments and personal obligation or calculation questions are outside it. A source-based calendar with invented amounts remains a teaching example, rather than a determination of compliance.

03

Count only transfers received before each payment

The first payment occurs before the March month-end transfer. Only the January and February transfers have arrived by March 16. The reserve therefore holds CAD 8,000 immediately before that payment: CAD 6,000 initially plus two CAD 1,000 transfers.

After paying CAD 5,000, CAD 3,000 remains. Before the June payment, five transfers have arrived in total, while one instalment has already left. The second payment leaves CAD 1,000. By September 15, eight transfers have arrived and two instalments have been paid, leaving only CAD 4,000 before the next CAD 5,000 bill.

The first unfunded event is therefore September 15, with a CAD 1,000 shortfall. A transfer scheduled for the end of September cannot fund that earlier payment unless another source has been arranged. The stepped chart retains every payment and transfer date so this timing remains visible.

04

The final annual deficit can understate the earlier funding need

Four entered instalments total CAD 20,000. Twelve reserve transfers total CAD 12,000. Starting cash of CAD 6,000 produces a negative CAD 2,000 reserve after the final December transfer. That is the annual reconciliation, but it is not the lowest balance.

The December instalment is due before the December month-end transfer. At that payment date, only eleven transfers have arrived. The lowest modeled balance is negative CAD 3,000. The extra cash needed at the beginning to keep every event funded is therefore CAD 3,000, bringing the required starting reserve to CAD 9,000.

The additional December transfer improves the year-end balance after the shortage has already occurred. This is why simply dividing an annual funding gap by twelve or looking only at the last account balance may not give a workable payment plan.

05

Test the starting reserve beside the ongoing transfer

The matrix varies opening reserve and monthly transfer while retaining the four selected payment amounts and the fixed 2026 dates. Every cell reruns the event calendar and reports additional cash needed at the start. It measures a funding gap, not an amount of tax saved.

A larger monthly allocation can reduce the extra starting cash required, but it does not make the allocation affordable. Reconcile it with regular expenses, other debt payments and the household’s emergency reserve. Money already promised to another goal is not simultaneously available for instalments unless that goal’s plan changes.

Different confirmed instalment amounts can also change which payment date produces the lowest point. Entering zero for one payment is merely an arithmetic input; the calculator does not decide whether omitting that payment is permitted. Keep the confirmed tax requirement separate from the cash-plan experiment.

06

Reconcile actual payments with the tax record

  1. Confirm the applicable instalment obligation, amounts and dates independently.
  2. List the cash already reserved and the dates of future transfers.
  3. Check the account balance immediately before each payment.
  4. Allow for the payment method’s processing and receipt timing.
  5. Record confirmed payments separately from internal saving transfers.
  6. Reconcile those payments with the relevant tax record and later return.

The model earns no interest and calculates no instalment interest, penalty, final annual tax, refund or balance owing. A remaining reserve is still household cash; it is not automatically a tax overpayment. Recheck the current official rules before using the dates for an actual payment, particularly when the year, jurisdiction or personal circumstances differ from this fixed example.
